item.title: Powering the AI Revolution: The Future of Data Centers with Ben Lee
item.dc:creator: Justin Nachea
item.description: Original ArticleThe latest episode of Penn Engineering’s Innovation & Impact podcast features Benjamin Lee, Professor in Electrical and Systems Engineering […]
item.content:encoded:
Original Article
The latest episode of Penn Engineering’s Innovation & Impact podcast features Benjamin Lee, Professor in Electrical and Systems Engineering and in Computer and Information Science. Lee’s research explores computer architecture, microprocessors, memory systems and data centers, with a focus on energy efficiency and environmental sustainability.

In this episode, host Vijay Kumar, Nemirovsky Family Dean of Penn Engineering and Professor in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics, speaks with Lee to examine the growing physical and environmental costs of artificial intelligence, from the electricity and water required to run data centers to the hardware that powers increasingly complex AI models. The conversation explores how advances in chip design, computing architectures and data center operations could make AI more efficient, as well as the challenges of keeping resource consumption in check as demand accelerates.

Lee also discusses the relationship between computing infrastructure and energy systems, the trade-offs involved in reducing carbon emissions and why engineering research will be essential to scaling AI more sustainably. As AI capabilities continue to expand, he considers how incremental advances across chips, data centers and electricity generation could significantly improve efficiency over time.

Listen to a cross-disciplinary conversation about AI, computer engineering and the future of sustainable computing.

Subscribe to Penn Engineering’s Innovation & Impact podcast on Apple Music, Spotify or your favorite listening platforms, or find all the episodes on our Penn Engineering YouTube channel.

item.title: Ten years of innovation, entrepreneurship, and impact at Pennovation Works
item.dc:creator: Justin Nachea
item.description: Marking a decade of helping companies launch, grow, and attract investment, Pennovation Works, the University’s 23-acre innovation hub, aims to […]
item.content:encoded:
Marking a decade of helping companies launch, grow, and attract investment, Pennovation Works, the University’s 23-acre innovation hub, aims to sustain and scale its groundbreaking work to foster a next generation of discovery in fields like AI, robotics, life sciences, and quantum science.

Original Article

After earning three degrees at Penn—his bachelor’s, master’s, and doctorate—Matt Piccoli co-founded his company, Vertiq, in a former mailroom in about 50 square feet of space.

The company, which today designs motors and control software for unmanned aircraft systems, was an early startup at Pennovation Works, which opened 10 years ago this fall in a former paint and chemical manufacturing space.

“The team made it very easy for us to land in an office and grow our company when we transitioned from prototype to product,” Piccoli said.

Pennovation Works, Penn’s innovation hub, was an early entrant into the incubator space in Philadelphia, helping companies such as Piccoli’s develop ideas, form partnerships, and bring ventures to commercialization.

At the start, said Michael Borda, associate vice provost for research and executive director of strategic initiatives, the Pennovation concept was straightforward. “Bring a bunch of smart people together. They would start talking, and these happy collisions would happen,” Borda said. The brief to founders, he added, was similarly simple: “Get going. Do what you do best.” Then Pennovation would reduce the barriers to make sure they could do that.

‘Ideas to impact’

Ten years later, those once-simple ideas have grown to support hundreds of companies that have together raised more than $1.1 billion.

“Over the past decade, we’ve seen startups learn, partnerships take shape, and discoveries move from ideas to impact,” said Denita Henderson, managing director of Pennovation Works, located on 23 acres that includes labs, offices, and production space in the Grays Ferry neighborhood of Philadelphia.

The space

50,000 square feet: Pennovation Center, an incubator space

65,000 square feet: Pennovation Lab, a multi-tenant laboratory for companies that no longer need an incubator

21,600 square feet: Inventor Office Building, a flexible workspace

Speaking to a crowd at a recent 10th anniversary celebration, Henderson said: “Today is really about both looking back and looking ahead, reflecting on what we’ve built together, and thinking about what’s next for innovation, entrepreneurship, and our region.”

John Swartley, Penn’s chief innovation officer, recalled that 20 years ago, before Penn had even purchased the property, the University’s “innovation ecosystem” was not well connected and while the quality of the research was high, “the means by which you could identify and then move and liberate those who made meaningful impacts … was just broken,” Swartley said.

The University’s solution was Pennovation Works, spurred on with enthusiasm and the support of Penn leadership at the highest levels. “Innovation is a team sport,” Swartley said. “You need to have all the equipment, and all the facilities, and you need to have the arena. If you don’t have the important pieces of that continuum, you continue to stumble.”

‘Window into the future’

When the center opened a decade ago, Philadelphia had a shortage of lab space, and the new complex was fully occupied at opening, Borda said. He noted that one of its advantages is the membership structure, which allows a company to start operations without signing a 50-page lease agreement—a deliberately low barrier to entry.

At the opening in 2016, the new venture was described as an “iconic new landmark and Penn’s window into the future,” said Anne Papageorge, senior vice president for facilities and real estate services.

Pennovation Works, she said, “has created a model for how ecosystems can serve as engines of economic growth and societal progress.” The hub aims to translate discoveries into products, ventures, and services “to real-world application to improve how we live,” she added.

The timeline

2010: Penn purchases the 23-acre former DuPont Co. paint production facility

2014: Groundbreaking for the Pennovation Center

2016: Pennovation Works’ grand opening

When companies graduate from Pennovation to go to alternate locations, ultimately to continue to grow, it can be celebrated and recognized as a success story, speakers said at the celebration. Borda suggested that Pennovation’s purpose is to give young companies the environment and resources to develop. Outgrowing the environment and continuing to scale is evidence that the model is working, he said.

‘Penn really led that pivot’

Jen Gilburg, deputy secretary for technology and entrepreneurship in Pennsylvania’s Department of Community and Economic Development, said Penn “really led that pivot to innovation, and then filing patents, and now commercialization. … Penn has been on the forefront of that.”

The first decade of Pennovation, said Executive Vice President Mark Dingfield, proved that the concept can work; the challenge of its next 10 years is to sustain and scale the investment.

“We need to stay focused on this as young companies scale and some of the best ideas in the region grow up here,” he said. “The breakthroughs that we see ahead are not specific to any one field. It’s going to be at the intersection of AI, robotics, life sciences, quantum, and this is really a place where those intersections, those points of creative friction, can develop.”

The numbers

$1.1 billion: Amount raised by Pennovation Works’ tenants over the last decade.

100+ companies today call Pennovation Works home

90 founders have been helped by the Pennovation Accelerator since 2017, raising nearly $90 million in funding.

More than 200 Philadelphia students have gone through the Youth, Entrepreneurship & STEAM (Y.E.S.) Initiative in the last year.

Watch the Pennovation Works’ Innovation and Impact Summit on the occasion of its 10th anniversary celebration.

item.title: AI platform allows real-time conversation between patients and their medical devices
item.dc:creator: Justin Nachea
item.description: Original ArticleA new AI-driven platform could allow people to interact with their medical devices by sending messages using a smartphone […]
item.content:encoded:
Original Article
A new AI-driven platform could allow people to interact with their medical devices by sending messages using a smartphone application and receiving feedback in real time. Participants in a proof-of-concept study undergoing monitoring for seizures could ask questions about their brain activity, receive personalized alerts, report symptoms and behaviors, and help train the system to better recognize seizure-related patterns.

The platform represents a fundamental shift from today’s medical devices, which largely collect data that is reviewed periodically by clinicians, to systems that actively collaborate with patients to manage their health, according to findings published today in Nature Medicine by researchers at the Perelman School of Medicine and the Center for Neuroengineering and Therapeutics (CNT) at the University of Pennsylvania.

“The idea is that instead of waiting for a specialist to analyze the data collected by your device, the device could detect changes and alert you immediately, like your own personal Jiminy Cricket on your shoulder,” said senior author Brian Litt, MD, a professor of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Bioengineering. “More importantly, both the patient and the device can learn together over time. The device learns what matters to the patient, and the patient learns how their behavior affects their health.”

Turning data into conversations

To test the new model for patient-device communication, researchers enrolled 13 adults undergoing continuous brain monitoring using electroencephalogram (EEG), in Penn’s Epilepsy Monitoring Unit (EMU). These individuals were admitted for monitoring for a number of reasons, including determining the source of their seizures, or as part of pre-surgical evaluation.

The participants tested a platform, constructed by a team of Penn Bioengineering PhD students, led by Zack Goldblum, Haoer Shi and Zhongchuan Xu, which consisted of three components:

  • Software that continuously captured EEG data from electrodes in the participant’s brain;
  • A secure, HIPAA-compliant cloud environment that analyzed incoming information in near real time;
  • A smartphone application featuring a Penn-developed, AI-powered conversational agent, similar to the technology used for ChatGPT.

Through an app on their phone, patients could ask questions about their brain activity, request visualizations of trends in their data, report symptoms, and receive alerts or surveys throughout the day. Patients could receive information such as text, charts, and other visual formats. Similarly, the device could contact the patient when it saw changes that might be of interest to the patient, and learn “on the fly” based upon patient responses.

Researchers analyzed 1,307 messages exchanged between patients and the system during the study period. Most interactions involved discussions about seizure events, sleep, mood, energy levels, and other factors that can influence seizure activity.

Patients were also surveyed three times daily about sleep, anxiety, mood, well-being, and other symptoms. Several participants said the platform helped explain patterns they had previously observed but struggled to understand.

One participant reported that the system helped “solidify what I felt to be true between some of my episodes and emotions.” Others said they valued access to sleep information and the possibility of receiving warnings before major seizures.

Beyond this communication, patients could also teach the system about their condition, noting which seizures the program correctly identified, and which were false alarms. This allowed the system to substantially improve its ability to accurately identify seizures. Clinicians could also converse with the system to review the program’s assessments and add in their own notations of true seizures and false alarms, further improving its accuracy. This was done via a smart “expert in the loop” algorithm that reduced the need for expert input to high-value annotations.

As systems become more personalized, researchers believe they will require rare clinical supervision, making them practical for long-term outpatient use.

A platform for the next generation of medical devices

Although the study focused on epilepsy, the team believes the platform could have broad applications for conditions that use cardiac devices, insulin pumps, and emerging treatments for neuropsychiatric disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder, addiction, and cognitive disorders.

In the future, researchers envision systems that can automatically adjust treatment while communicating directly with patients about symptoms and treatment goals. The team is already preparing studies with Lauren Hammer, MD, PhD, an assistant professor of Neurology and Bioengineering, that will apply the platform to automatically tune deep brain stimulation devices used to treat Parkinson’s disease. Further work is incorporating wearables to applications for insomnia, epilepsy, brain and vital signs monitoring.

“Patients often understand aspects of their disease that sensors cannot measure directly,” Litt said. “Imagine an insulin pump that can answer questions about how a meal will affect blood sugar, or a Parkinson’s device that adjusts treatment based on how a patient feels during a walk or writing a letter. We envision medical devices becoming partners in care that learn alongside patients and help them make better decisions every day.”

Researchers believe this type of two-way communication could fundamentally change the relationship between patients and medical devices. Rather than serving as passive monitoring tools, future devices could continuously combine physiologic signals, patient feedback, and AI-driven analysis to deliver more personalized and responsive care.

The work builds on Litt’s broader effort to develop a new generation of brain-computer interfaces capable of sensing physiologic signals, communicating with patients, learning from their responses, and adapting treatment in real time, and is supported by a $5.6 million NIH Pioneer Award (DP1 NS122038-01).

Ongoing research will evaluate whether the platform can reduce seizure frequency and severity, improve quality of life, decrease emergency department visits, and lower health care utilization. Researchers also plan to expand testing into outpatient settings using newer minimally invasive EEG and wearable technologies designed for continuous monitoring during daily life.

item.title: A Delaware hub dedicated to ‘Human-AI cooperation’ launches with $21.5 million to study AI in healthcare
item.dc:creator: Justin Nachea
item.description: Original Article Scientists at a new Delaware research hub envision a future where AI-powered sensorsassess a patient’s injury from the […]
item.content:encoded:
Original Article

Scientists at a new Delaware research hub envision a future where AI-powered sensorsassess a patient’s injury from the moment they enter an exam room.

As the patient climbs onto the table, the system detects a subtle tremor that might otherwise go unnoticed.

Backed by a five-year,$21.5 million federal grant, the NSF AI Institute for Human-AI Cooperation (HAIC) will focus specifically on applications like these in physical therapy and healthcare.

The team includes researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and the University of Delaware who are working to design AI technologies that can help with decision-making, monitoring of symptoms, and other aspects of care.

They imagine a clinical environment where the provider, patient, and AI system are all working together.

“We are not trying to replace people in any way,” said Eric Eaton, the managing director of the institute and a research associate professor at Penn. “This is an opportunity to really explore how AI can become an adaptive teammate.”

Experts in computer science, AI, robotics, physical therapy, medicine and ethics work in tandem at the institute, which celebrated its launch with a ribbon-cutting last Wednesday. The collaboration also includes Delaware State University, Princeton University, and the University of Florida.

Headquartered at the University of Delaware’s Newark campus, it is the 30th AI research institute nationwide established by the U.S. National Science Foundation.

The institute will also focus on workforce development and designing courses and degree programs at the intersection of AI and health.

“We want to achieve the ultimate goal of personalized healthcare,” said Cathy Wu, the director of HAIC and a professor in the computer & information sciences department at the University of Delaware.

Learning to cooperate

In the field of AI, “alignment” refers to the practice of designing AI to match human goals, intentions, and decision-making.

“We want to make sure that the human is in the driver’s seat,” Wu said.

The researchers envision AI getting incorporated as a partner, rather than a replacement for clinicians.

In physical therapy, AI-powered sensors could help the physical therapist recommend the best set of exercises, and adapt those exercises as the patient recovers.

AI could also monitor patients as they perform exercises independently, to “get the complete picture,” Eaton said. A physical therapist managing multiple patients at once may be unable to monitor each one throughout a session.

As a patient walks on a treadmill, for example,AI-powered motion-tracking cameras could continuously evaluate their movements.

In the exam room, sensors could measure how well a patient’s knee injury is healing, starting when the patient enters the room. As the patient climbs onto the bed, the sensors could detect a subtle tremor that might indicate Parkinson’s disease.

“If no one else was in the room with you, that would never have been noticed at all,” he said.

By tracking changes over time, an AI system could help assess cognitive decline or signs of depression.

AI could also identify a patient’s concerns and ensure that the provider addresses each one before the visit ends. It could pull up relevant medical records in real time — for example, locating a test the patient had two years ago that could be relevant.

The researchers will work on developing the foundational AI technologies to support these scenarios. At the same time, they will work with stakeholders and ethicists on AI guardrails.

“I don’t want to build a system that I wouldn’t be comfortable using in a clinical exam room,” Eaton said.

Guardrails

The institute will study how to integrate AI into healthcare without compromising patient privacy or the doctor-patient relationship.

For example, the system could convert the image of a person walking into a privacy-preserving skeleton or wire-frame.

Researchers may also develop training to help healthcare workers understand the nuances of AI, including “when to trust it, when not to,” Eaton said.

An AI tool that provides recommendations or decision support for the clinician must be clear on its level of confidence and access to relevant medical information, as well as any uncertainty in its recommendation.

Doctors should be able to examine the system’s decision-making process and verify that it is auditable, Eaton said.

The same principle applies to the need for patients to understand how AI reaches its conclusions.

Stakeholder advisory boards will help the institute ensure its technologies address these concerns.

“We need to bring a lot of checks and balances,” Wu said.

item.title: Harnessing technology to help farmers assess crop health earlier
item.dc:creator: Justin Nachea
item.description: As the fall harvest arrives, Cherie Kagan and Akhila Mallavarapu of the Penn-led Internet of Things for Precision Agriculture center […]
item.content:encoded:
As the fall harvest arrives, Cherie Kagan and Akhila Mallavarapu of the Penn-led Internet of Things for Precision Agriculture center explain how 1-cent biodegradable sensors could tell farmers how their crops are doing long before the yield comes in.

Original Article

Every meal has a story that begins long before it reaches the plate. No matter what it is, parts of it trace back to the soil—some constituent component was planted, grown, and harvested at a farm. Even the seemingly unnatural qualifies; neon cheese puffs began life as corn, and gummy worms owe their wiggle to a syrup pressed from the same.

Behind every bite is a farmer who spends a season making calculated bets about water, fertilizer, and pests, hoping for a bountiful harvest without ever having a complete picture of what’s happening on each plant or beneath the soil.

“There’s a lot of competition for land that you could farm. You’re not going to get more of it,” says Cherie Kagan, the director of The Internet of Things for Precision Agriculture (IoT4Ag)— a National Science Foundation Engineering Research Center led by Penn. “You have to make the most of what you have—not ruin the fields, not waste resources.”

Add mounting threats like aflatoxin, a fungal contaminant locking U.S. peanuts out of foreign markets, and the bacterial greening disease hollowing out Florida citrus, and farming’s oldest problems intensify—by the time a cornfield yellows, the damage is done, and the fall harvest is jeopardized.

IoT4Ag seeks to give farmers a better picture of their harvests before it’s too late.

“We want to make the invisible visible,” says Kagan, who is the Stephen J. Angello Professor of Electrical and Systems Engineering in the School of Engineering and Applied Science and holds a secondary appointment in the Department of Chemistry at Penn’s School of Arts & Sciences. “It’s like preventative medicine.”

Penn leads a team with researchers from Purdue University, the University of Florida, and the University of California, Merced, so the technology can prove itself across different crops, climates, and regulations.

Planted like seeds, stuck on like tape

Commercial soil-moisture probes can run $2,000 apiece, says Kagan, who has a secondary appointment in the School of Arts & Sciences. On one Florida farm the researchers visited, that meant a single sensor was stretched hundreds of acres, leading to massive blind spots. The IoT4Ag team set out to engineer sensors that cost a fraction of that, aiming for around one cent per unit.

The team built tiny biodegradable devices that were sowed with the same planters as the seeds. Beneath the soil surface, they answer radio frequency pulses to report root-zone moisture and chemical conditions back to operators.

Above ground, former Kagan Lab postdoctoral researcher Akhila Mallavarapu builds leaf sensors—flexible, adhesive stickers.

These sensors can be applied by robotic arms or sprayed directly onto foliage, and each sticker changes to give a visual readout of leaf-surface humidity, pH, or the volatile compounds emitted by a stressed plant.

Eyes on every leaf

Autonomous ground robots developed in the lab of Penn Engineering Dean Vijay Kumar read these optical leaf sensors. While drones rely on visible leaf yellowing under bright midday skies, these robots are equipped with onboard lighting and can therefore operate day or night.

Kagan notes that standard agricultural machinery such as tractors, sprayers, and center-pivot irrigators can also be retrofitted with optical cameras to scan leaf stickers during routine farm operations.

Researchers in Cherie Kagan’s lab at Penn Engineering test IoT4Ag’s sensing technology, from adhesive color-changing leaf sensors to measurements at the optical bench, and outdoors alongside a campus weather station.

At Penn, this multi-departmental effort brings together multiple Engineering faculty including Kevin Turner (sprayable leaf sensors and printed soil sensors), Troy Olsson, (soil sensors), Mark Allen, (biodegradable batteries), and Pratik Chaudhari (field imaging).

Once captured, field signals must cross rural connectivity gaps where cellular service is patchy or nonexistent. To solve this, the Purdue team engineered the Solar-Powered Remote IoT4Ag Network Gateway (SPRING). Using tripod-mounted, solar-powered gateways, SPRING transmits field metrics directly to cloud servers.

Growers can deploy the software within their own cloud accounts, keeping full ownership of their operational data. Analytics developed across all partner institutions present growers with actionable recommendations through user-friendly, chat-style AI interfaces.

No new homework

“If it’s too complicated, they just won’t use it,” Kagan says.

But complication isn’t the only barrier. Farmers “have to trust you to put your tech in their livelihood, and you have to prove it won’t take too much of their time,” she says, noting that growers are fiercely protective of their daily operational schedule.

To that end, the center builds around tools growers already have, leaning on the dozen growers on its advisory boards. Those voices steer the center’s research and three “joint operations”: optimizing nitrogen, optimizing water, and mitigating disease and pests.

From test bed to seed stage

The hardest acre to cross may be the one between the labs and market, the researchers note. “Once we get the sensors working in the lab, the next step is demonstrating value to growers,” Mallavarapu says.

With IoT4Ag renewed for four more years of NSF funding, it will provide resources for more sensors and field trials of new sensor technologies. Mallavarapu was recently named an Activate Fellow, supporting Vividence Labs—her startup commercializing the leaf sensors to flag crop stress days before damage shows.

Kagan says the ultimate objective of the center extends beyond developing novel nanomaterials or field robotics or AI—it’s about building integrated systems that address global challenges in food, energy, and water security. It’s about making a positive impact on society.

Ultimately, it is about making a positive impact on society, she says. “We do science, we learn something new, and then we ask: What is it good for? What can we make from it that actually helps people?”

Cherie R. Kagan is the Stephen J. Angello Professor in the Department of Electrical and Systems Engineering with secondary appointments in the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at Penn Engineering and the Department of Chemistry in Penn Arts & Sciences. Kagan is also director of the Internet of Things for Precision Agriculture Engineering Research Center.

Akhila Mallavarapu is a former postdoctoral researcher in the Kagan group at Penn Engineering and co-founder of Vividence Labs.

This work received support from the U.S. National Science Foundation (Award EEC-1941529) and the Goldsmith Sustainable Agriculture Fund at the Kleman Center for Energy Policy.
